Written by the Dharma-brother Bhikṣu Zhengyin, Abbot of Yuyang Chan Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture, in honor of his late Master.
This master truly never spoke such words. Take care not to transmit them as if they were carved upon a printing block. May readers understand this.
"The opening of the mouth does not reside on the tongue. The Way of our former Master has thus been propagated.

Nine prostrations from the Dharma-heir Bhikṣu Jizu, Abbot of Shanquan Chan Monastery in Changzhou Prefecture, together with his wife, Lady Shao Miaozhen, who have contributed pure wealth for the embroidery and carving of this edition. Former Attendant Officer of the Court of Ceremonial, Zhang Weixin.
Written by the monk Juehui, Keeper of the Archives at Tiantong Wanshou Chan Monastery in Jiaxing Road;
and the Abbot Wanjin of Tiantong Wanshou Chan Monastery in Jiaxing Road.
By the connection of causes and conditions, [there was] the Yuan Dynasty Grand Master of the Middle Rank, Fohai Puyin Guangci Yuanwu Dashi...
Biographical Record of the Venerable Chan Master Zhong:
The Master’s name was Shouchong; his courtesy name was Tanfang. He was born on the first day of the tenth month in the year of Yihai of the Zhiyuan era into the Huang family of Duchang, Nankang.

At the age of nine, he resolved to leave the household life, but his mother would not permit it. His relatives then exhorted his mother, and she finally allowed him to fulfill his aspiration. At [the monastery of]... (text continues).
He received the tonsure at age twelve under Chan Master Zhencui of Yushan at Yunju. Having received full ordination, he traveled abroad;
upon reaching Jiangshan, he stayed for two summer retreats. He attended the lectures of Tianxi Guanjiang, where he listened to the *Lotus Sūtra* and understood it immediately upon hearing it.
Master Fuguang, who presided over the lectures, marveled at his brilliant insight and hailed him as a person of "reincarnation. At that time, Master Tienshan Qiong’s path...
He caused a stir throughout the Wu region. He went there to seek instruction and visited Master Yigong of Mount Meng. The Master asked where he was from, and the teacher replied, "Duchang.
Yigong asked, "Did you come by boat or by land? The teacher replied, "I have not traveled by either. Yigong extended both hands, and the teacher stared at them with wide-open eyes.

Subsequently, they lived together at Xiuxiu Hermitage. After some time, he paid his respects to Master Fugong of Huyan at Mount Jing, where he served as the head of the monastic administration for one term.
In his later years, he went to see Master Ri at Dongyan to take charge of the library, but did not accept the position. He then visited Master Yu at Lingyin;
when Yu raised the koan regarding the cypress tree in front of the hall, the Master’s doubts were entirely resolved upon hearing the words.
Taking his leave, he returned to see Master Ruyu at Haili in Linjiang, where they rejoiced greatly together. He subsequently traveled to Chongyin in Jinling, where Yuanfeng Hong... [text ends].
Duke [Tughan] welcomed him to reside in the first seat. When Fēng moved to Bǎo'íng, the assembly recommended the Master to succeed him on the throne. He opened the hall as the successor of Yùshān.

In the spring of the *xīnyǒu* year of the Zhìzhì era, the Chancellor of the Jiangzhe Provincial Secretariat, Duke Tuóhuān, who was presiding over the Administration of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs (Xing Xuānzhèng Yuàn), transferred the Master to Jiāngshān.
In the first month of the *yíchǐ* year of the Tàidìng era, the temple was destroyed by fire; however, the Crown Prince...
When the Prince of Liang arrived in Jinling, he climbed the mountain the following day and asked the Master, "Since the temple has been destroyed by fire, upon what does the Buddha now rely?
The Master replied, "The Buddhas of antiquity have passed away; the Buddhas of the present have returned. He asked again, "How will it be restored?

The Master replied, "It relies on the presence of a great donor. The Prince nodded his head in agreement. The following year, copper was smelted to cast a great bell. The Prince understood the meaning of the gesture.
The green pearl, once the [stupa] was completed, remained perfectly within the bell. When the inscription "Long Live the Emperor! was added, its color became even more brilliant and lustrous.
The King and the Master ascended Mount Baizhu (Pearl Peak) and saw that the rear slope was level and expansive, with dense and luxuriant forests, suitable for establishing a monastery (*saṃghārāma*).
He ordered stones to be piled up to mark the site. On another day, he personally took up a spade to break ground, whereupon gold and silk coins emerged. He made [offerings of them].
He inscribed the characters "Chongxi" (Venerable Happiness) by hand as the plaque for the temple hall. Not long after, the Prince was displeased during his journey to Jiangling.

The Master prayed to Master Bao on his behalf and obtained an auspicious result. The Prince pointed toward heaven and the sun, vowing that he would repay the divine favor. Subsequently, he returned home.
He ascended the Great Jewel Throne; he was Emperor Wenzong.

In the autumn of the first year of the Tianli era, he dispatched an envoy to the mountain to confer upon Master Bao the title "Dao-lin Zhen-jue Ci-ying Hui-gan Pu-ji Sheng-shi" (The Holy Teacher of Universal Salvation, Whose Compassionate Response and Wisdom are Responsive, the True Awakened Forest of the Path).
Furthermore, he bestowed the title "Fo-hai Pu-yin Da Chan-shi" (Great Zen Master of the Universal Seal of the Buddha-Ocean) upon Zhugali and changed the name of Chongxi to Chongxi Wanshou.
He was granted one collection of the scriptures, five hundred taels of white silver vessels, fifty taels of gold, and two *naqshid* banners.
At that time, the former imperial residence was renamed the Great Longxiang Jiqing Monastery. By imperial decree, the Office of the Censor-in-Chief was to select a founder for the monastery;
the Master was chosen for this role, but he declined the honor, proposing instead the Venerable Xin from Central India to take his place. This was in the second year.
In the spring, the Master was conferred the title of Grand Master of the Middle Rank (Dazhong Dafu) and named Great Chan Master Guangci Yuanwu.
He served as the abbot of Chongxi Jangshan and presided over the administrative affairs of the construction projects.

In the autumn of the first year of Zhishun, Zhao Shian, the Minister of the Imperial Censorate, transmitted an imperial decree summoning the Master and Master Yin of Longshuo to the capital. On the ninth day of the ninth month, the National Preceptor Miaozong presided.
Wang Shihong, the Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, was introduced at the Quanzhang Pavilion. He was granted a seat and received inquiries regarding his welfare.

The Daxi Zongyin Court was ordered to provide him with daily provisions and meals. He was bestowed with a gold-threaded robe and a sable fur cloak; those who accompanied him, including Jiao and others, were likewise granted gifts according to their rank.
Subsequently, he had an audience with the Empress and the Crown Prince, receiving lavish and cordial treatment. He then visited the Imperial Preceptor, who presented him with [gifts].
The Tibetan tribes presented tribute rice. Subsequently, he received an imperial decree to offer incense at Mount Wutai; on that day, auspicious light appeared.
Upon his return, he submitted a memorial, and was granted a *naqshīsh* monastic robe. On the New Year’s Day of the second year, he attended the Daming Hall and was bestowed a golden-embroidered robe.
When the Emperor was in Jinling, he once asked the Master about thin *jiang* porridge and three pairs of socks; now, he asked again. The Master replied as before.
The Emperor looked toward the court historian Yu Ji and ordered him to record this, and further commanded Ji to compose the inscription for Jiangshan Temple.

On the □□ day of the third month, [the Emperor] submitted a memorial requesting the restoration of the horse-stable manor lands that had been seized by powerful commoners, and subsequently petitioned to return to the mountains.

The Emperor firmly urged him to remain. Although he declined as many as four times, the Emperor then ordered Zhang Jinkia Nu, the Palace Attendant, to host a banquet at Sheng’an Temple under the supervision of the Grand Minister Sadi.
Imperial vessels were provided and the arrangements were most magnificent. On the following day...
He was granted one hundred *ding* of paper currency and one hundred taels of white silver. The Imperial Preceptor presented him with furs, garments, woolen hats, and other items as parting gifts.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Grand Minister of the Interior Zhao Shian was dispatched to grant another five hundred *ding* of paper currency, ten post-horses, and two official carriages;

he was further commanded that all local offices and military garrisons along the route provide escort. Having returned to the mountain, he used these endowments to extensively undertake construction projects.

The lofty towers and magnificent halls seemed as though they had descended from heaven. Before long, the Imperial Preceptor dispatched Han Jianu, Director of the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs, to bestow five thousand *ding* of paper currency and fifty *qing* of reclaimed fields in Pingjiang.
He also remitted the land taxes for the two monasteries.

By imperial decree, the two generals Su Shi and Shang Liu, along with the painter Zhao Yuanpan—all men of national renown—were commissioned to fashion images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and deities. These three were all [eminent figures of the] state.

As for the hand, it could not have been obtained without imperial decree. When the Emperor ascended to the realm of the immortals, the Master established a Water and Land ritual for seven days and nights to offer him posthumous merit.
On the evening of the concluding ceremony, as the Master ascended the seat to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma, there was an auspicious sign of nectar.
At the beginning of the current Emperor’s accession to the throne, there were frequent imperial edicts of praise and protection, as well as the bestowal of gold and silk.
Furthermore, the Empress Dowager granted one hundred taels each of yellow and white gold, twenty taels of Yunnan gold, two hundred strings of paper currency, and twenty rolls of patterned brocade.
In the spring of the first year of Zhizheng, he retired to Longpan Hermitage. The following year, Duke Gao Nalin...

The Director of the Imperial Academy first invited the Master from Mount Jing; after three successive missions, he finally consented to depart. The temple had long been in decline and burdened by accumulated arrears, yet the mountain was majestic.

When the local officials and their clansmen heard that the Master had arrived, they vied with one another to provide grain and provisions for his sustenance. His disciples numbered more than two thousand.

In the spring of the fifth year, the Year of Yiyou (1365), the Provincial Administration Bureau received an imperial decree to transfer the Master to reside at Longxiang, under the auspices of the Chancellor of Jiangzhe, Dorji.

The Duke personally issued an earnest invitation. That very day, [the Master] boarded the imperial carriage and traveled to Jinling, where the assembly followed him until there was no room left for them.
The following year, he petitioned the court for retirement and resided at Guangci Hermitage, awaiting his summons. In the seventh month, the temple caught fire.

At that time, Duke Gao served as the Grand Official of the Administration Commission (Xingtai Dafu) and exhorted the Master, saying: "This was the former Emperor’s private residence; among the temples of Jiangnan, it is the foremost. Now..."
The temple was destroyed. Who but a master could restore it? The Master said, "It is my duty to see this through. He then purchased timber on a large scale and assembled the craftsmen;

all the buildings were constructed simultaneously, and they were completed within less than two years. On the twenty-eighth day of the tenth month in the eighth year, the Wuzi year (1368), he was afflicted by a slight illness.
He summoned his disciples and said, "You must exert yourselves in my Way so as not to bring shame upon the State."
He encouraged his family with these words of devotion: "Exert yourselves! I am departing. On the day before his passing, he wrote this verse:
"This stinking skin-bag, Is unobstructed wherever it meets the eye. Once dead, it shall be burned and buried; There is no need to compete with others.

The various offices of the provincial government each presented memorial offerings, and the common people led the way in providing funds for a seven-day assembly. Those who came to offer incense from their heads and arms as an act of devotion were numerous.

The carriage containing the reliquary emerged from the eastern gate. The entire city turned out with music and performance; those who escorted him numbered tens of thousands. The fire for the cremation was five-colored.

The Grand Officer Xing Ji Gong ordered ten thousand households to station troops to guard the perimeter. When the fuel was exhausted, the cranial bone, teeth, eyeballs, and prayer beads were all found intact.
The śarīras were beyond counting. Wherever the smoke reached, the trees and forests became covered in clusters of growth, as if they had been grafted.

[The wood] was joined together; even firewood-gatherers and herdsmen took branches from it to sell in the market. His disciples, Daichen and others, enshrined [the remains] at the Dragon-Coiled Immovable Pagoda.
Daji and others further divided the pagoda and established one at the foot of Mount Lingxiao on Mount Jing.

The Master stood seven chi and five cun tall; he was magnificent and imposing. His voice resonated like a bell. In his daily life he spoke little, yet whenever he did speak, every word was an instruction. King...

The Duke was a man of noble rank; upon hearing his introductory discourse but once, people could not help but bow their knees. Whenever he left the precincts of the government offices, the scholars and commoners vied with one another to welcome and prostrate before him, fearing they might be late;
they hailed him as the "Living Treasure" (Huobao Gong). In instructing his disciples, he did not mince words or soften his expression, earning him the nickname "Iron Face.
Nevertheless, everyone felt a deep personal affinity for him. When composing verses for social occasions, he never drafted them beforehand; he would simply take up paper and write with great speed.
His calligraphy was characterized by a rigorous, upright, and majestic style, as can be seen in the *Wuhui lu* (Record of the Five Assemblies).

When the Master first traveled to various regions, he journeyed together with Master Zhuyuan Sheng; later, Zhuyuan retired to a mountain hermitage in Huaixi, where his Way resounded greatly throughout the age.

Whenever the Master wished to cross the Yangtze River but was unable to do so, he would repeatedly offer portions of his bestowed goods to support him. Furthermore, he recommended Zhuyuan for the abbacy of Jiangshan to serve as his own replacement.
The Master resided at Chongyin for fifteen years and at Jiangshan for twenty years. Regarding all matters concerning the temple’s funds and grain, he never intervened;

he simply allowed the administrative officials to manage their expenditures and receipts. Consequently, surplus wealth accumulated in great abundance. When the Master departed, his successors began to exercise stricter control over the finances, and the storehouses gradually began to dwindle.
One day, on the Treasure Street (Baohua Jie), there was a man leading a sheep to the slaughterhouse. Upon seeing this, the Master paid double the price for it.

He released them into the various mountains. Tu immediately changed his occupation. From then on, many officials and nobles frequently released sheep, deer, geese, and pheasants at the Master’s location, calling it "releasing living beings" (fangsheng).
When the Huayan Pavilion at Mount Jing was destroyed by fire, hundreds of rooms were consumed by the flames.
He restored the site to its former state and made it even more magnificent than before; this was the second reconstruction since the time of Longxiang.

He emptied his own purse and provided five hundred strings of cash as an initial offering, and he did the same for the project at Mount Jiang. This is why donors place their trust in him and why such undertakings are so easily accomplished.
The Master was diligent in serving the community, ensuring that the four requisites were provided in abundance and excellence, while he himself wore tattered robes and ate coarse food.
He ate with an air of profound simplicity. Initially, Emperor Wenzong had thought that the Master’s attire and provisions would necessarily be luxurious;

one day, however, he went out incognito and went straight to the Master’s inner chamber, where he found nothing but torn paper curtains and a bedding of coarse paper. He departed with deep admiration.

Although the Master did not devote himself to secular classics, once something passed before his eyes, he never forgot it for the rest of his life; even as for the *Shiji*, he was able to recite it from memory twice over. Thus he spoke.
Whenever he composed a piece, he would lift his pen and not miss a single character. Duchang was a neighboring district of our region of Wupu;
the Master’s clan resided on its borders, very close to my own family. While the Master resided at Longxiang, I joined the ranks of his disciples for three years.
Regarding the excellence of his master’s virtue, learning, speech, and conduct, these were indeed witnessed and heard directly by him.
In recent times, the records of great venerable masters have often been produced by men of noble rank or prominent figures;

such individuals, however, allow their personal likes and dislikes to influence them, resulting in deletions and alterations that compromise the truth. Now, at the request of his disciple Renxing, the abbot of Cuiwei in Piling, [I have compiled this].
I have therefore recorded directly what I have heard and seen regarding his greatest deeds, not daring to offer a single word of praise or censure.

It is my hope that future generations may have something upon which to rely and place their trust. During the Master’s lifetime and on the day of his passing, there were many miraculous and auspicious signs.
Omissions were not recorded due to concerns regarding heterodox elements.
Written on the eighth day of the second month in the spring of the ninth year of Zhizheng (Jichou), by the monk Kexin, a student of the Dharma;
calligraphed by Liu Zhen, Grand Master of Central Harmony and Administrative Officer of the Censorate for the Propagation of the Law throughout the Jiangnan Provinces.
Epitaph for the Late State Preceptor Zhong, the Great Zen Master Fogai Puyin Guangci Yuanwu,
Elder of the Great Longxiang Jiqing Monastery.
On the twenty-eighth day of the tenth month in the year of Wuzi, the eighth year of the Zhi Zheng era, the Great Zen Master Guangci Yuanwu...
He passed away in the quarters of the Great Longxiang Jiqing Monastery. One day prior, he summoned his disciples and left behind this verse:
"This stinking skin-bag, Is unimpeded wherever it meets the eye. Once dead, it is burned and buried; Do not seek to compete with others.
The following morning, he addressed them again, saying: "From this day forward, you must all be courageous and diligent, so as to perpetuate and flourish [the Dharma]."
"May I not fail the mind of our Imperial Court, which has held my teaching in such high esteem," he said, before departing with a serene air.
After a short while, his countenance and spiritual radiance shone brilliantly like golden light.

His remains stayed in the shrine for seven days, during which time the Grand Censor of the Southern Circuit, Duke Xingji, led the various civil and military offices in presenting offerings. All those who cherish virtue likewise paid their respects.

They exhorted one another to contribute funds to hold a seven-day and seven-night vegetarian assembly (*śrāddha*). Some offered their own bodies as lamp-wicks or incense for their heads and arms, exhausting their utmost sincerity and reverence in making offerings.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month, the reliquary (*stūpa*) departed from the eastern city gate.

The officials prepared the ceremonial rites with accompanying music, and tens of thousands followed in the procession. Some wore hempen garments and leaned on staffs, wailing and lamenting in grief, as if they were returning from a journey.

There was something miraculous about this: as the cremation was nearly complete, the wind shifted and the smoke coalesced, forming a five-colored canopy directly above the stupa of Master Bao, suspended clearly in mid-air.
When the wood was exhausted and the fire extinguished, there were countless five-colored śarīra relics.
Wherever the smoke had touched the trees, śarīra adhered to the leaves like pearls; the larger ones were the size of soybeans. Furthermore, śarīra appeared within his skull bone, teeth, and eyeballs.
The rosary he previously held remained entirely intact. His disciples, including Dachen and others, enshrined it within the Acala Stūpa at Longpan Hermitage.
Furthermore, Jingshan Daqi and others divided the stūpa and established it below Lingxiao Peak.

Having reached fifty-six years of monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) and seventy-four years of worldly age, his disciples, including Fuyu, the abbot of Yuyuan, respectfully submitted this letter and—
Xingshi came from Liuzhou and requested me to compose an inscription for his stupa. Unable to decline, I have thus composed this preface and its inscription.
The Chan Master’s name was Shouzong; his courtesy name was Tanfang. He was the son of the Huang family of Huangjin in Duchang, Nan-kang, Jiangxi. At birth, he manifested many spiritual wonders.
At the age of nine, he earnestly aspired to leave the secular world, but his mother would not permit it; he consequently refused to eat for several days, causing concern among his relatives.
He repeatedly requested permission from his mother, who then acceded to his wish. He took Yunju Yushan Zhen Chan Master as his teacher.
At the age of eleven, he shaved his head and received full ordination. His appearance was imposing and dignified, and his spirit was transcendent. He traveled extensively throughout all quarters.

He went to Mount Jiangshan and stayed there for two years. Upon arriving at Tianxi Monastery, he served as a lecturer; he listened to lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra* and other scriptures until he fully understood their meanings.
While he was residing at the mountain, Dharma Master Foguang recognized his potential and said to the assembly, "This man is truly one who has returned from the beyond.
He then entered the region of Wu, where he paid homage to Master Zhen of Jue’an at Chengtian Monastery, met Master Qiong of Tieshan, and encountered Master Yi of Mengshan at Xiu.
Xiu. Master Yi asked the Master his native place. The Master said, "Duchang, Jiangxi. He asked, "Did you come by boat or by land?

The Master replied, "I have not traversed either path. Master Yi spread out both hands; the Master stared at him with wide-open eyes, and they subsequently lived together. After some time, he went to Jingshan to see Master Fu of Huyan.
Upon seeing him, Master Fu recognized his extraordinary potential and appointed him to oversee the monastic administration for one year. Thereafter, he went to Yuyuan.

The Master saw Master Riguang at Dongyan. Riguang declined the invitation, preferring to remain in charge of the Tripitaka collection. He encountered Master Zhuyuan Sheng, with whom he traveled together past Xuedou.
There they met Master Tongwu Tong, under whom they spent the summer retreat. In the autumn, they returned to Lingyin to visit their teacher, Yushan.

One day, while entering the inner quarters for instruction, the Master raised the following case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou replied, "The courtyard..."
Previously, when the Master [Zhaozhou] spoke of the "cypress tree in the courtyard," [Fayan Wenyi] attained sudden and great enlightenment upon hearing it once with his faculty of hearing.

Fayan granted him formal certification (*inka*). After some time, he went to Huili Temple in Linjiang to see Master Haiyin Ru. He traveled among various Chan masters, and his words and spiritual resonance were in perfect accord;

wherever he went, he was held in high esteem. He returned again to Jiankang and occupied the seat beside the master at Chongyin Temple to instruct his disciples. It happened that Master Hong of Yuanfeng was being promoted.

The assembly recommended Chan Master Baoning to succeed him on the seat; he then opened the hall to preach the Dharma, thereby continuing the lineage of Yushan, thus adhering to the fundamental principles of the source and its branches.
Consequently, his reputation for the Way grew increasingly weighty.

In the spring of the Xinyou year of the Zhizhi era, the Left Chancellor of the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration, Duke Tuohan—who was presiding over the Office of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs—having long heard of the Master’s noble conduct, invited him to reside at Jiangshan.
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month in the year of Yichou (1325) during the Taiding era, Prince Liang arrived in Jiankang. That evening, the temple was struck by a disaster.
The following day, the Prince visited the temple and asked the Master, "How shall we restore it? The Master replied, "We rely on the presence of a great donor.
The Prince nodded in agreement. The following year, they cast a great bronze bell, for which the Prince offered a precious pearl as a donation.
Once it had entered the smelting furnace and was completed, the precious pearl shone brilliantly within the inscription on the bell that read "Ten Thousand Years, [Longevity to] the Sovereign.

Again, he asked the Master, "Since the temple has been destroyed, upon what does the Buddha rely for his dwelling? The Master replied, "The Buddhas of antiquity have passed away; the Buddhas of the present have returned once more."
The King was greatly delighted. One day, the King and the Master ascended Mount Maṇigiri. Seeing clouds and mist rising from behind the peak, they descended to that spot.
Surveying the surrounding forest foothills, which were deep and beautiful, the King said to the Master, "This is a suitable place for a vihāra."
He ordered his attendants to stack stones to mark the site. On another day, when the King returned, he personally took up a hoe and commanded the Master to recite a verse.
The King then thrust the hoe into the earth to break ground and bestowed wealth upon it, entrusting the Master to construct a Buddhist temple named Chongxi (Venerable Joy).
He had the two characters "Chongxi" inscribed in large script and ordered the Master to remain at the monastery; from then on, whenever the King visited, he invariably stayed there.

In the *Lianwenbian* (Connected Questions and Debates), he frequently cites sayings from the Chan school as questions. One day, the King asked the Master, "What is meant by the 'coarse gruel of Jiang' that these patch-robed monks speak of?
The Master replied, "I thought Your Highness had forgotten. The King asked again: The Master replied, “I thought Your Highness had forgotten. The King asked again:
"What is meant by the 'three pairs of socks' of the Zen monks? The Master replied:

"Having traversed all the mountains and rivers within the realm, this morning I have personally arrived at the palace of the Brahma King. The King was struck with silent realization; they gazed at one another and attained harmony.
In the autumn of the first year of the Wuchen cycle, the King ascended the Great Throne and changed the era name to Tianli. The Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing incense in a casket.

Upon arriving at Mount Jiang, he paid his respects to Master Baogong and thanked him for his hospitality. On the eve of this visit, the Master had dreamed that a divine being bestowed upon him a seal.
Rising early the next morning, an envoy arrived to grant him a golden brocade *kāṣāya* and bestow upon him the title of Great Zen Master Fohai Puyin.
Furthermore, the temple Chongxi was renamed Dachongxi Wanshou Temple, and he was granted a complete set of the Buddhist canon (*piṭaka*) along with five items of silverware.
One hundred *liang* [of silver]; fifty *liang* of gold; and two *nashi-shi* banners.

There was an imperial decree stating that the Great Longshuo Jiqing Temple should be constructed at the former residence of the Jinling Prince. The Emperor commanded the Chan Master to be the founding patriarch (*kaisan*).
The Master recommended the Elder Daxin from Central India to take his place. Upon reporting back, he met with the Emperor's approval. In the spring of the second year, the Emperor dispatched...

An imperial edict was issued, specifically conferring upon the Master the title of Grand Master of the Second Rank (Dazhong Dafu), the Great Chan Master of Universal Compassion and Perfect Enlightenment (Guangci Yuanwu Dacianshi).

He was appointed as the Abbot of the Great Chongxi Wanshou Monastery and concurrently in charge of the Jishan Taiping Xingguo Chan Monastery, serving as the Director of Works for the reconstruction of the Jiqing Wanshou Monastery.
In the first year of the Zhishun era, Zhao Shian, the Censor-in-Chief, transmitted an imperial decree summoning the Master.
Together with the Great Dragon Xiang Yin, he traveled by imperial post to the capital.

Upon arrival, the National Preceptor Miaozong and the Minister of Personnel Wang Shihong escorted him for an audience with the Emperor at the Quanzhang Pavilion. The Emperor granted him a seat and questioned him warmly.
He was ordered by the Daxi Zongyin Yuan to provide daily meals and provisions, with various allowances distributed to his attendants as well. An imperial decree was issued.

The Empress Dowager and the Crown Prince visited him. He commanded the Grand Master Shi Ming, the Chancellor Zhao Shiyen, and the Palace Attendant Zhang Jinniaonu to prepare exquisite delicacies to provide against the severe cold.
The Emperor bestowed a sable fur robe upon the Master, and all those accompanying him were granted garments and cotton.

They went to have an audience with the Imperial Preceptor (Ti-shi), who received them with the utmost honor; he presented them with the "Imperial Rice" offered by the people of Tibet. Shortly thereafter...

By Imperial Decree, he was granted an audience with the Chan Master Zhikong of Xitian. Accompanied by Master Xun, he traveled to Mount Wutai on imperial mission to pay homage to the Great Being Mañjuśrī;
beholding auspicious radiance, he returned and presented his report, which met with the Emperor’s approval. He was bestowed a *naqshish* (納失失) monastic robe.

On the first day of the New Year in the second year, the Xinwei year, he attended the Daming Hall and was granted a gold-embroidered *kaṣāya*. By Imperial Order, Scholar Yu Ji was commissioned [to compose the inscription].
He composed the "Record of the Re-establishment of Jiangshan Temple" and wrote large characters for the signboards of Guangci Hermitage and various other halls.

On the eighteenth day of the third month, he submitted a memorial requesting leave to return home. The Emperor insisted on retaining him, but as he would not desist in his request, the Emperor finally granted his plea.
He addressed the Master by his courtesy name and expressed his appreciation. The Emperor then ordered the Palace Attendant to prepare a grand banquet at the Imperial Study to bid him farewell.
The Imperial Temple was granted vessels from the Inner Treasury and musical performers. Furthermore, the Grand Minister Sadi was ordered to preside over the banquet.

The following day, one hundred *ding* of Zhongtong paper currency and one hundred taels of white silver were bestowed. An edict was issued through the Tongzheng Yuan to provide ten postal horses and two state carriages.
The Imperial Preceptor presented a vermilion hat, a Buddhist robe, and one set each of silk fabrics for both the outer and inner layers. [He] requested Jiang...

To the various temples of the south: To uphold the imperial decree, on the fifth day of the fourth month, by special imperial edict, the rent and grain taxes for the fields of Jiangshan were remitted.

On the eighth day, His Majesty dispatched the Grand Councilor Zhao Shian to bestow another five hundred *ding* of Zhongtong currency upon the Master, commanding him to carry incense in a casket and return to the mountain.
Subsequently, the Director of the Xuanzheng Yuan, Han Jianu, was sent to grant an additional five hundred *ding* of currency.
Qian Ding was dispatched, along with Zhao Yuanpan and the two generals Shang and Liu, to sculpt and paint images of various Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and deities;
all were works of unsurpassed artistry for their time. In the autumn of the fourth year, the Guiyou year, the Sovereign passed away.
The Empress Dowager, following the will of the late Emperor, dispatched envoys twice, bestowing one hundred taels each of gold and silver, as well as twenty taels of refined gold from Yunnan.
He received two hundred *ding* in cash and twenty rolls of patterned silk.
At the beginning of the Yuantong era, when the present Emperor ascended the throne, he was granted an imperial letter accompanied by imperial incense, gold, and silk.

On the first day of the third month in the first year of the Zhizheng era (*xinsi*), the Chan Master ascended the hall, struck the drum to assemble the congregation, and spoke a verse to bid farewell to Jiangshan before returning home.
Lóngpán Ān was intended as his place for spending his final years. In the third month of the second year, a *fúróng* tree in front of the hermitage suddenly burst into full bloom;

everyone was astonished. In the fourth month, the Left Chancellor of the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration Commission, Bieqier Puhua Gong, and the Director of the Xuanzheng Yuan, Nalin Gao Gong, dispatched an imperial messenger bearing a memorial from the provincial administration and the court to invite the Chan Master to reside there.

At Jingshan, the Chan Master’s refusal was most firm; yet as those who requested his presence were unceasing, he eventually consented to go. He remained there for three years and achieved significant results.

When he again took his leave, the Imperial Secretariat and the Court supervised the local authorities to ensure his ascent with due ceremony and earnestly entreated him to stay. In the first month of the fifth year, he departed once more.
The present Emperor, by special decree, commanded the Chan Master to ascend to the abbacy of Dàlóngxiáng Jíqìng Temple.
An envoy was dispatched with incense to formally invite him. The Zhōngtái Dàfū Yìliánzhēn, along with the various offices of the Shěng and Yuàn, all submitted formal petitions to this effect.
He was escorted to Jiānkāng on official vessels. In the third month of the sixth year, the Chan Master retired to reside at Guǎng...
At Ciana (Ci-ān), he awaited imperial edicts. The officials of the Imperial Academy (Naituan) led the local authorities to petition him four times, increasing their efforts;

yet the Chan Master declined resolutely as before. In the seventh month, a disaster struck the temple. Nalin, the Grand Officer of the Southern Academy (Nantai Dafu), led his subordinates to Guangci-an and said to the Master:
"In all the temples built in Jiangnan since the founding of our dynasty, this is the only one that has been so magnificent. Now that it has met with such a calamity..."

"Who could restore this place if not one possessed of the power of the path, practice, and vows? Moved by compassion, the Chan Master reflected upon the profound kindness of the late Emperor and immediately rose to take charge of the monastery’s affairs.
First, he offered his robes and alms bowl to purchase timber and employ craftsmen, undertaking the reconstruction from the beginning. In the seventh year, the temple was completed.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of the eighth year, the *wuzi* cycle, the Chan Master ascended Mount Jiang to pay homage at the stupa of Master Bao.

Cibao Gong said that [the Master] had come and gone between Jinling for over forty years, as if there were a karmic affinity from a previous life with the Great Being (Mahāsattva), and that he had relied upon him for his entire life.
Passing by Longpan Hermitage, he entrusted the affairs of the hermitage to his disciples Qiwei and others, and then returned to Longxiang.
This was exactly one day prior to the date of his passing. — Chan Master Zhiyuan.
His practice was perfected; his consciousness was lucid and his learning pure. His speech was concise yet essential, and his responses were calm yet timely.
He composed verses and hymns that were free from the exaggerated and bombastic rhetoric of the Chan school, instead embodying the straightforward and sincere intent of the patriarchs.
In his past endeavors, he eliminated long-standing abuses and renewed the tradition. His Dharma assemblies flourished to match those of famous monasteries. While residing at Jiangshan, he...

It has existed for the longest duration of years. Although the temple was ravaged by fire, through the power of his vows, halls, pavilions, gates, corridors, and other buildings—numbering several thousand bays in total—were restored with magnificent beauty.
Within less than a month, tens of thousands of long-standing debts were settled, and the granaries and treasuries became overflowing.
All the construction work was completed, and the number of monks in the monastic quarters reached one thousand seven hundred. He preached the Dharma and practiced [the path].
The Way possesses a brilliance that illuminates the past. Its monastery, Dàlóngxiáng, was again struck by fire. The former design was magnificent, and its construction had required vast expenditures;
it truly relied upon the labor of the people. Now, the Chan Master has undertaken its reconstruction, with expenses provided from the monastic treasury (chángzhù) and labor supplied through hiring.
Thus, the ancient vision has been fully restored. The assembly deems this a difficult feat. It is as [the restoration of] the Great Being Bǎogōng, or like the one posthumously titled Shèng Pǔjì.

The Master was granted a pearl-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe and twenty precious vessels. Furthermore, regarding the Arhat’s property that had been submerged at Sima Village, it was all petitioned for by the Chan Master.

As for the fields of Meishan Huayan Fushou Daci and others, which had been mortgaged to wealthy commoners over many years, the Chan Master managed them all to restore them to the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika-vastu*). Greatly auspicious!
The Emperor granted fifty *qǐng* of fields in Pingjiang and remitted the taxes on the reed marshes; these were also the result of the Chan Master’s expositions.

Regarding the achievements he accomplished throughout his life and the honor and favor bestowed by the Imperial Court, others could not help but admire them, yet the Chan Master harbored no intention of self-display even as much as a hair’s breadth.
All the gifts he received were returned to the public, and the surplus from his almsgiving was...

Whenever he encountered those who were destitute, he would immediately provide for their urgent needs. On the day he entered parinirvāṇa, all that remained were his three robes, a towel, and an alms bowl, along with a few items such as ancient curiosities and books.
As for Chan Master Su from Yushan, he was the fifth-generation Dharma descendant of Chan Master Songyuan Yue;
the disciples he ordained, who transmitted the Dharma and resided on the mountain, numbered several dozen. Various regions prepared [offerings].
He attended to several people. His disciples compiled his posthumous writings, titled the *Wuhui Lu* (Record of the Five Assemblies), which has circulated in the world.
Regarding the Zen Master’s life experiences, he did not retain them in his mind; yet, as for the radiant light at the end, he was able to foreknow it.
Fearing that his disciples might harbor ambitions to emulate others, he thus composed a four-line verse at the time of his passing, wherein the first two lines disparaged his illusory body.
The final two lines exhort one not to compete. With what would one compete? The Master’s intent is profound. The inscription says:

"The vast waters of the marsh flow surgingly, nurturing excellence and gathering auspicious signs. Mount Zhong rises majestically, harboring blessings and storing wonders. For a thousand years, the vital energy has gathered."
I rely solely on the Master to bring this about. Whether he bestows gold upon me or appoints me to office, I dare not refuse such an appointment nor decline such a gift.
For wealth and honor reside in Heaven; how could they be known by me? Not being base is my nobility; not being poor is my wealth.

Since these are not something I must seek through self-debasement or self-pennury, they are what I inherently possess. My vows for the five assemblies resound mightily throughout all quarters, proclaiming: "This is the power of our Buddha. Heaven...
The radiance of the son. Alas for that moon! It traces back to the sun and possesses brilliance. The essence of the sun presides over death; Heaven does not deviate from this.

That Heaven does not deviate, and that nature is not obscured, manifests the original substance of the moon—perfectly full and upright. I inscribe this for the ancients, taking the ancient moon as my witness.
The Buddhas appear before me; they do not undergo annihilation. A dragon coils amidst the soaring clouds; there stands a stūpa. Master.
I have no desire for competition; my inscriptions are already numerous.
